notes:
I've put together verse-by-verse notes on Job 24 below. Some gaps first, so you know what's missing:

- **Searches I couldn't fill:** I couldn't run separate searches for Orthodox sources (oca.org), Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), Pentecostal sites other than Enduring Word, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. My searches and page fetches ran out first. Separate searches might still turn something up.
- **Not found:** I found no Protestant traditions disagreeing along denominational lines on this chapter. The real disagreements are about how to read the text, and they cut across traditions. Where it helps, I note each writer's background: Gill was Baptist; Clarke and Benson were Methodist; Matthew Henry and Poole were Puritan or Nonconformist; Guzik (Enduring Word) is Calvary Chapel. Those labels come from what I already know, not from the pages.
- **Catholic material is thin:** It's limited to Haydock's introduction to Job and the Vulgate readings that Protestant commentators mention.
- **Some links have no citation tags:** The Pulpit Commentary page and the Biblehub Job 24:1 page were read in full, but they came back without the markers that citation tags need. Points from them carry only the URL.

---

**Overview: whose voice is speaking?**
- Commentators agree the chapter is hard. Andersen, quoted by Guzik, lists three problems. Many lines are nearly unreadable in the Hebrew. The speech can seem disjointed. Some of it sounds more like Job's friends than Job. "In chapter 24 we run into all kinds of problems. First there are textual difficulties, which render many lines almost unintelligible… Secondly, the speech as a whole seems incoherent to many readers… Thirdly, chapter 24 is said to express sentiments that Job could never have uttered. They would sound better on the lips of his friends." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-24/
- Coffman (via StudyLight) notes that a number of verses are rejected and removed by different scholars; but there's no agreement on any of this. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/24-1.html
- Matthew Henry's summary: Job accepts that the wicked will suffer after death. What he utterly denies is his friends' claim that ordinarily they are miserable in this life. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_024.cfm
- **Catholic (Haydock):** He says the book's aim is to shew that the wicked sometimes prosper, while the good are afflicted. Job's views can't be condemned, because God called them right. The friends held a false opinion, and Haydock says they are even considered as the forerunners of heretics. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/job.html

**v. 1**
- **Guzik:** The sense is roughly: since God knows everything and will judge it all, why are the godly left in the dark about His ways? "Since God knows and will judge everything, why are the godly kept in the dark about His ways?" https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-24/
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The "times" are God's set occasions for acting as moral ruler of the world. He defends the righteous and punishes sinners, like the prophets' "day of the Lord." Even God's faithful servants aren't told when those days will come, and that troubles Job. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/24.htm
- **Barnes:** Job doesn't doubt that God sees everything. His question is why God doesn't step in and treat people as they deserve. Job's only answer is to look to a future reckoning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/24-1.htm
- **Benson (Methodist) and Poole:** "His days" means the times God sets for punishing the ungodly. If punishment always came in this life, good people would surely notice it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/24-1.htm
- **Gill (Baptist):** The verse follows from Job 23:14. God has decreed all things, so the times for carrying them out can't be hidden from Him. Gill also reports that several Jewish commentators read it as a wish: "why are not times hidden?" https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/24-1.html
- **JFB:** Those who truly know God long for the day of the Lord. Not being told the times tests their faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/job-24.html
- **Older Latin and Greek readings:** Barnes reports that Jerome made the verse a statement: times are not hidden from God, but those who know Him don't know His days. The Septuagint reads it differently again. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/24-1.htm
- **Hebrew note:** Biblehub's study notes say *mishpat* ("judgment") carries the sense of a set time for a court session. https://biblehub.com/job/24.htm

**v. 2**
- **Pulpit:** Fields had no fences, so low boundary stones marked who owned what. Moving them was an easy form of theft. Stolen flocks were mixed into the thief's own herd and grazed openly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/24.htm
- **Guzik, quoting Bradley:** The law curses anyone who moves a neighbour's landmark (Deut 27:17). Yet "Job sees no curse fall!" https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-24/
- **NET Bible notes:** The Hebrew line has no subject, so translators add "wicked men." The LXX reads "and their shepherd." Many commentators accept this reading. But the MT says that they graze the flocks that they have stolen. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=job&chapter=24&verse=2
- **Clarke (Methodist):** He notes Good's alternative translation, "they destroy" rather than "they feed." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-24.html

**v. 3**
- **Pulpit:** The fatherless were easy targets because they had lost their protector. Taking a widow's ox as a pledge may not have been illegal, but it was still oppression. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/24.htm
- **Guzik:** Eliphaz had accused Job of exactly these sins (Job 22:5–11). Job agrees this is how the wicked behave but denies he is one of them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-24/

**v. 4**
- **Pulpit gives two readings:** the powerful make the poor step aside on the road, or they make the roads so dangerous that the poor take back paths. Pulpit prefers the second. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/24.htm
- **Gill:** He offers moral, social and literal senses. The "poor of the earth" are also poor in spirit, and they hide together out of fear. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/24-4.html
- **Clarke's application:** He warns that those who *wink* at tolerated oppression *leave the world worse than* *they found it*. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-24.html

**vv. 5–8: who is the "they"?** Commentators genuinely disagree here.
- **The robbers:** Pulpit takes vv. 5–8 as the raiders, roaming the desert like wild donkeys. In vv. 7–8 they put up with cold and rain because they're set on plunder. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/24.htm Barnes reads v. 6 the same way, as living off plunder. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/job-24.html
- **The victims:** On v. 7, Barnes describes people stripped and left exposed to the desert's cold nights. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/job-24.html Coffman says the oppressors force their poor laborers who work for them to scavenge for food in the mountains, where they have no residences, and are not sufficiently clothed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-24.html
- Biblehub's summary also follows the BSB, picturing the poor scavenging, gleaning in their oppressors' vineyards and sheltering against rocks. https://biblehub.com/job/24.htm
- **v. 6, JFB:** Read as "belonging to the wicked," the phrase implies that only the wicked own vineyards and the godly poor have none. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/job-24.html
- **v. 8, an old sermon application:** The *Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary* turns the "rock" into a picture of Christ. They say a rock only gives shelter if you run to it and cling to it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/24-4.html

**v. 9**
- **Pulpit:** This is a different set of oppressors, town-dwellers. They seize a debtor's nursing baby as payment and make the child a slave (compare 2 Kings 4:1; Neh 5:5). They also take the poor person's clothing in pledge. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/24.htm
- **Clarke:** Children are taken to be raised as slaves. A new paragraph starts here. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-24.html
- **Smick, quoted by Guzik:** These pictures show Job's contempt for wickedness and his sympathy for people in distress. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-24/

**vv. 10–11**
- **Pulpit:** The poor man's only cloak was taken in pledge, so he goes almost naked. He carries his oppressor's sheaves while starving, and presses oil and wine while thirsty. The KJV's wording of v. 10b is wrong. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/24.htm
- **Gill:** The sheaf may be what the poor had gleaned ear by ear, and even that is taken. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/24-10.html
- **Coffman:** Refusing workers a taste of what they harvest goes against the spirit of Deut 25:4. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-24.html

**v. 12**
- **Clarke:** The scene moves from the countryside to the city, where the miseries are too many to list. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-24.html
- **Matthew Henry:** "God layeth not folly to them" means God doesn't punish them at once or make an example of them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/24-1.html
- **Barnes:** God lets the wickedness go unpunished (compare Acts 17:30). Job's point isn't that God ignores the cry of the afflicted. It's that He doesn't step in against tyrants. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/job-24.html
- **Guzik:** This is the part Job found hard to accept. Smick adds that God's later speeches would teach Job a lesson about this. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-24/

**v. 13**
- **Pulpit:** These people reject the light of reason, conscience and law, linked to John 1:9. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/24.htm
- **Clarke:** They rebel against God's light in conscience and in His word. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-24.html
- **Matthew Henry gives two readings:** a figurative rebellion against nature, God's law and conscience, or literal people who avoid being seen. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_024.cfm
- **Biblehub note:** Rebelling against "light" (*or*) is rebellion against God Himself. https://biblehub.com/job/24.htm
- **Guzik** compares Romans 13:12 on casting off the works of darkness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-24/

**v. 14**
- **Pulpit:** The killer rises at first light and attacks poorer houses. Theft is his main aim; he kills if he is resisted or discovered. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/24.htm
- **Gill:** He robs and kills at dawn, steals at night, and may especially target God's poor saints. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/24-14.html

**v. 15**
- **Pulpit:** Moral darkness and physical darkness go together, as in John 3:19–21. The adulterer also hides his face. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/24.htm
- **Gill:** He compares the adulterer to an ostrich (citing Tertullian), or a child covering his eyes, who thinks no one sees him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/24-15.html

**v. 16**
- **Pulpit:** Burglars dug through weak clay or brick walls. He prefers the reading "they shut themselves up by day" to "marked for themselves." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/24.htm
- **Barnes** agrees: probably "in the day time they shut themselves up." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/24-16.html
- **Gill** prefers burglars marking houses by day, but notes the other reading. He also applies "know not the light" to rejecting God's word and God Himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/24-16.html

**v. 17**
- **Pulpit:** They hate the morning because it means being caught, and being caught means the gallows. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/24.htm
- **Barnes:** The point is they're at home in deep darkness and fear only daylight. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/job-24.html
- **Clarke** applies the verse especially to the adulterer, afraid of being recognised. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-24.html
- **Matthew Henry:** When they are recognised, their own consciences accuse them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_024.cfm

**vv. 18–20: Job's own view, or his friends' view?** This is the main interpretive split.
- **Pulpit** calls v. 18 very obscure, saying some regard him as giving his own judgment on the ultimate fate of the wicked; others, as anticipating what his opponents will say on the point. It also reports a theory about river pirates. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/24.htm
- **Guzik:** These are "should" statements. Job is telling God how He ought to judge the wicked, in this life as well as the next. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-24/
- **Job quoting his opponents:** One commentator on Biblehub's v. 18 page says Job quotes the opinions of his adversaries ironically. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/24-18.htm The Layman's Bible Commentary takes the same line, with vv. 21–25 as Job's reply. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/job-24.html
- **Coffman** mentions the view that vv. 18–25 belong to Bildad's speech, but thinks the text as it stands fits Job. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-24.html
- **v. 18, Barnes:** Their "portion" means their way of earning a living, which deserves to be cursed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/job-24.html
- **v. 18, Cambridge Bible (via Biblehub):** The tyrant is like foam on the water, quickly swept away. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/24-18.htm
- **v. 19, Pulpit:** As summer heat dries up snowmelt, Sheol swallows the wicked. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/24.htm
- **v. 20, the "womb":** NET says "womb" stands for the mother. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php/verse.php?book=Job&chapter=24&verse=20 Clarke suggests "mercy" instead: when mercy itself forgets the sinner, his ruin is certain. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-24.html
- **v. 20, the death itself:** Barnes reads it as an ordinary death with no special sign of God's displeasure. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/job-24.html Matthew Henry agrees: the man is buried like anyone else and forgotten. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_024.cfm Benson, by contrast, says even the man's mother would be ashamed of him after such an accursed death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/job-24.html

**v. 21**
- **Bullinger, quoted by Guzik:** A barren wife was more helpless than a widow, who might at least have sons. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-24/
- **Gill** discusses several readings and settles on oppressing childless women who have no one to defend them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/24-21.html
- **Clarke** follows the Vulgate, "he feedeth the barren." He takes it to mean the man is kind to the barren but no friend to large families. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-24.html
- **Pulpit:** Neglecting the widow means failing to defend her cause, which was an accepted duty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/24.htm

**v. 22: is "He" God, or the tyrant?**
- **God:** The BSB, Guzik and Biblehub's summary take the subject as God dragging down the mighty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-24/ ; https://biblehub.com/job/24.htm
- **JFB reverses it:** God *prolongs* the life of the mighty. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_024.cfm
- **The tyrant:** Pulpit, Gill and Barnes take "he" as the tyrant, who draws powerful allies to his side. Gill mentions the Jewish commentator Jarchi (Rashi), who reads it as God dragging the wicked to punishment, but Gill prefers the tyrant reading. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/24.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/24-22.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/job-24.html

**v. 23**
- **Pulpit and Gill:** God grants the wicked man safety, he leans on it, and God's eyes are on his ways. Pulpit adds that the wicked seem to be under God's special care. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/24.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/24-23.html
- **Ellicott:** The eyes may be the tyrant's, though taking God as the subject also makes good sense. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/24-23.htm
- **Clarke:** A tyrant relies on guards he doesn't trust. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-24.html
- **Catholic (Vulgate):** Gill reports that the Vulgate reads "God gives him place of repentance, and he abuses it to pride", and that the Targum is similar. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/24-23.html
- **Guzik:** Job reminds himself that God isn't blind to the wicked. He compares Psalm 73. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-24/

**v. 24: does this describe an easy death, or judgment?**
- **An easy death:** Barnes says they aren't cut off violently or early. They are like grain left standing until harvest (compare Ps 73:4). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/24-24.htm JFB says they get a *quick and easy death.* https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_024.cfm Pulpit says Job minimizes the terrors of their death, and exaggerates its alleviations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/24.htm
- **Judgment:** Clarke (Methodist) disagrees. Tyrants shall at last come to an untimely end. Few tyrants ever visit the eternal world *sicca morte*, but by a violent death. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-24.html
- **Benson and Poole:** Their success lasts at most one short life, so it isn't worth envying. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/24-24.htm
- **Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik:** In the East the harvesters cut off only the heads of the grain, "Thus will the wicked be cut off." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-24/

**v. 25**
- **Pulpit:** Job challenges anyone to prove him wrong, and this bold challenge no one attempts to take up. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/24.htm
- **Andersen, quoted by Guzik:** Job's position is more balanced, but more baffled. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-24/
- **Clarke's closing summary:** The friends said the righteous always prosper. Job answered that experience shows the righteous often suffer and the wicked often thrive. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-24.html
